claim: Temporal regularity is ubiquitous and essential to guiding attention and coordinating behavior within a dynamic environment.
source: Temporal regularity is ubiquitous and essential to guiding attention and coordinating behavior within a dynamic environment.
evidence: This is a general statement about temporal regularity that draws from established scientific understanding in the field of attention research.

claim: Previous researchers have modeled attention as an internal rhythm that may entrain to first-order regularity from rhythmic events to prioritize information selection at specific time points.
source: Previous researchers have modeled attention as an internal rhythm that may entrain to first-order regularity from rhythmic events to prioritize information selection at specific time points.
evidence: This claim references prior research models in the field, implicitly citing previous work on dynamic attending theory.

claim: Higher-order regularity based on rhythmic organization of contextual features (pitch, color, or motion) may serve as a temporal frame to recompose the dynamic profile of visual temporal attention.
source: Using the attentional blink paradigm, here we show that higher-order regularity based on rhythmic organization of contextual features (pitch, color, or motion) may serve as a temporal frame to recompose the dynamic profile of visual temporal attention.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript using the attentional blink paradigm.

claim: The attentional reframing effect is well predicted by cortical entrainment to the higher-order contextual structure at the delta band.
source: Critically, such attentional reframing effect is well predicted by cortical entrainment to the higher-order contextual structure at the delta band as well as its coupling with the stimulus-driven alpha power.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data showing correlations between delta-band entrainment and behavioral effects.

claim: The attentional reframing effect is well predicted by coupling between delta-band entrainment and stimulus-driven alpha power.
source: Critically, such attentional reframing effect is well predicted by cortical entrainment to the higher-order contextual structure at the delta band as well as its coupling with the stimulus-driven alpha power.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data showing phase-amplitude coupling between delta and alpha bands correlates with behavioral modulation.

claim: The human brain involuntarily exploits multiscale regularities in rhythmic contexts to recompose dynamic attending in visual perception.
source: These results suggest that the human brain involuntarily exploits multiscale regularities in rhythmic contexts to recompose dynamic attending in visual perception, and highlight neural entrainment as a central mechanism for optimizing our conscious experience of the world in the time dimension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that task-irrelevant contextual rhythms modulate attention.

claim: Neural entrainment is a central mechanism for optimizing our conscious experience of the world in the time dimension.
source: These results suggest that the human brain involuntarily exploits multiscale regularities in rhythmic contexts to recompose dynamic attending in visual perception, and highlight neural entrainment as a central mechanism for optimizing our conscious experience of the world in the time dimension.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined behavioral and neural data showing entrainment effects predict attentional modulation.

claim: People tend to utilize regularities in the sensory information flow for directing attention to the moments when a target event is expected to occur.
source: When it comes to the temporal domain, people tend to utilize regularities in the sensory information flow for directing attention to the moments when a target event is expected to occur (Nobre et al., 2007; Nobre and van Ede, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by Nobre and colleagues.

claim: After listening to a rhythmic tone sequence, auditory perception in terms of pitch judgment and time discrimination was more accurate for target tones appearing at the expected than the unexpected time points.
source: As a great example, Jones and colleagues have shown in a series of studies that after listening to a rhythmic tone sequence, auditory perception in terms of pitch judgment and time discrimination was more accurate for target tones appearing at the expected than the unexpected time points (Jones et al., 2002; Large and Jones, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies by Jones and colleagues.

claim: Facilitation effects from rhythmic attention have been extended to various aspects of visual perception and even across sensory modalities.
source: Such facilitation effects have been extended to various aspects of visual perception and even across sensory modalities (Bolger et al., 2014; Brochard et al., 2013; Mathewson et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2013; ten Oever et al., 2014), implicating the involvement of a general attentional selection mechanism guided by the regularity in stimulus timing.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dynamic attending theory assumes attention as an internal oscillatory activity (or attending rhythm) that can be entrained to rhythmic structures of the exogenous events.
source: These findings can be interpreted by the dynamic attending theory (DAT), which assumes attention as an internal oscillatory activity (or attending rhythm) that can be entrained to rhythmic structures of the exogenous events (Jones, 1976; Jones et al., 1981; Jones and Boltz, 1989; Large and Jones, 1999).
evidence: This claim describes the theoretical framework of DAT and is supported by citations to foundational papers.

claim: Electrophysiological research in humans and non-human primates have found entrainment of intrinsic neural oscillations to external stimulus rhythms.
source: In line with this assumption, electrophysiological research in humans and non-human primates have found entrainment of intrinsic neural oscillations to external stimulus rhythms, and regarded such process as an instrument for selective attention (Calderone et al., 2014; Obleser and Kayser, 2019; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: Neural entrainment creates 'temporal attentional spotlights' that attract the brain's attentional resources toward a string of selected moments.
source: Through neural entrainment, neuronal excitability aligns with the occurrence of rhythmic events, creating 'temporal attentional spotlights' that attract the brain's attentional resources toward a string of selected moments (Calderone et al., 2014; Henry and Herrmann, 2014; Lakatos et al., 2008; Lakatos et al., 2013; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on neural entrainment.

claim: When viewing a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) stream, there is a large chance that the observer would miss the second of two temporally proximate targets.
source: For instance, when viewing a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) stream, there is a large chance that the observer would miss the second of two temporally proximate targets, as the allocation of attention to the first target hinders the redeployment of mental resources to the second one (Broadbent and Broadbent, 1987).
evidence: This claim describes the attentional blink phenomenon and is supported by a citation.

claim: The attentional blink (AB) reveals the limitations of attentional allocation and memory processes that may become a bottleneck for conscious awareness.
source: This phenomenon, vividly referred to as the attentional blink (AB) (Chun and Potter, 1995; Raymond et al., 1992), has attracted much interest as it reveals the limitations of attentional allocation and memory processes that may become a bottleneck for conscious awareness (Dux and Marois, 2009; Martens and Wyble, 2010; Shapiro et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on the attentional blink.

claim: The AB effect poses a challenge in dynamic attending that cannot be circumvented solely by the anticipation built upon stimulus timing.
source: More intriguingly, as items in the RSVP stream are all rhythmically presented and temporally predictable, the AB effect poses a challenge in dynamic attending that cannot be circumvented solely by the anticipation built upon stimulus timing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that despite temporal predictability, the AB effect persists.

claim: The brain has to rely on regularities in the higher-order temporal structure of the information stream as a complement to the first-order regularity in rhythmic stimulation.
source: To address this challenge, here we propose that, the brain has to rely, as a complement to the first-order regularity in rhythmic stimulation, on regularities in the higher-order temporal structure of the information stream.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, which is then tested experimentally.

claim: If the endogenous attentional rhythm could entrain automatically not only to the stimulus rhythm but also to the higher-order structure based on the information content, the deployment of temporal attention might be reconstructed in a way that facilitates target detection in the AB task.
source: More specifically, if the endogenous attentional rhythm could entrain automatically not only to the stimulus rhythm but also to the higher-order structure based on the information content, the deployment of temporal attention might be reconstructed in a way that facilitates target detection in the AB task.
evidence: This is a hypothetical prediction that is tested in the experiments.

claim: The original AB stream had a stimulation rate at 10 Hz.
source: To test this hypothesis, we synchronized the original AB stream (stimulation rate at 10 Hz) to a hierarchical contextual stream that possessed a feature-based temporal structure—a 2.5 Hz rhythm arising from periodic changes of a physical feature, superimposed on its stimulus rhythm at 10 Hz.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and stimulus parameters.

claim: The hierarchical contextual stream possessed a 2.5 Hz rhythm arising from periodic changes of a physical feature, superimposed on its stimulus rhythm at 10 Hz.
source: To test this hypothesis, we synchronized the original AB stream (stimulation rate at 10 Hz) to a hierarchical contextual stream that possessed a feature-based temporal structure—a 2.5 Hz rhythm arising from periodic changes of a physical feature, superimposed on its stimulus rhythm at 10 Hz.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and stimulus parameters.

claim: Temporal structures defined by a variety of features (pitch, color, etc.) could regulate the dynamic deployment of visual attention so as to alleviate the AB effect.
source: Using temporal structures defined by a variety of features (pitch, color, etc.), we provided converging evidence that the structured context, which was task-irrelevant and even from a different modality, could regulate the dynamic deployment of visual attention so as to alleviate the AB effect.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main behavioral findings from multiple experiments.

claim: The structured context was task-irrelevant and even from a different modality.
source: Using temporal structures defined by a variety of features (pitch, color, etc.), we provided converging evidence that the structured context, which was task-irrelevant and even from a different modality, could regulate the dynamic deployment of visual attention so as to alleviate the AB effect.
evidence: This describes the experimental design where auditory contexts modulated visual attention.

claim: A robust AB effect was found for Experiment 1a.
source: Above all, we found a robust AB effect for Experiment 1a, as well as for the other experiments reported in the current study.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: A robust AB effect was found for all experiments reported in the current study.
source: Above all, we found a robust AB effect for Experiment 1a, as well as for the other experiments reported in the current study.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

source: The accuracy of T1 performance was very high in both the baseline session (mean ±SE: 0.959 ± 0.008) and the context session (0.953 ± 0.006), and the overall T1 performance ranged from 0.907 to 0.972 in all experiments.
evidence: This reports specific numerical data from the experiments.

claim: The T2 detection accuracy conditioned on correct T1 response was generally impaired in the short-SOA conditions relative to that in the long-SOA condition during the context session (t(15) = 5.443, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.361).
source: By contrast, the T2 detection accuracy conditioned on correct T1 response was generally impaired in the short-SOA conditions relative to that in the long-SOA condition (mean accuracy >0.9 for all experiments), during both the context session (t(15) = 5.443, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.361) and the baseline session (t(15) = 6.720, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.680).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the experiments.

claim: The T2 detection accuracy conditioned on correct T1 response was generally impaired in the short-SOA conditions relative to that in the long-SOA condition during the baseline session (t(15) = 6.720, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.680).
source: By contrast, the T2 detection accuracy conditioned on correct T1 response was generally impaired in the short-SOA conditions relative to that in the long-SOA condition (mean accuracy >0.9 for all experiments), during both the context session (t(15) = 5.443, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.361) and the baseline session (t(15) = 6.720, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.680).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the experiments.

claim: T2 was better identified when two targets appeared in two adjacent cycles (between-cycle condition) than within the same cycle defined by the background sounds (within-cycle condition) in the context session (t(15) = 2.947, p=0.010, Cohen's d = 0.737).
source: More importantly, looking close at T2 performance in the short-SOA conditions (Figure 1B), we found T2 was better identified when two targets appeared in two adjacent cycles (between-cycle condition) than within the same cycle defined by the background sounds (within-cycle condition). Notably, such difference was observed only for the context session (t(15) = 2.947, p=0.010, Cohen's d = 0.737) but not for the baseline (no sound) session (t(15) = −0.212, p=0.835, Cohen's d = 0.053), although the target positions were completely matched between these two sessions.
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 1B showing the data.

claim: The difference in T2 performance between between-cycle and within-cycle conditions was not observed for the baseline (no sound) session (t(15) = −0.212, p=0.835, Cohen's d = 0.053).
source: Notably, such difference was observed only for the context session (t(15) = 2.947, p=0.010, Cohen's d = 0.737) but not for the baseline (no sound) session (t(15) = −0.212, p=0.835, Cohen's d = 0.053), although the target positions were completely matched between these two sessions.
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the experiments.

claim: Only in the between-cycle condition, the contextual sounds enhanced T2 detection accuracy relative to the baseline (t(15) = 2.287, p=0.037, Cohen's d = 0.572).
source: Meanwhile, only in the between-cycle condition, the contextual sounds enhanced T2 detection accuracy relative to the baseline (t(15) = 2.287, p=0.037, Cohen's d = 0.572), while in the within-cycle condition, the performance kept comparable between the context and baseline sessions (t(15) = −0.271, p=0.790, Cohen's d = 0.068).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the experiments.

claim: In the within-cycle condition, the performance kept comparable between the context and baseline sessions (t(15) = −0.271, p=0.790, Cohen's d = 0.068).

claim: A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA yielded a significant interaction between experimental session (baseline vs. context session) and target position (between- vs. within-cycle) (F(1, 15)=7.151, p=0.017, ηp2 = 0.323).
source: The observed dissociation was further confirmed by a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, which yielded a significant interaction between experimental session (baseline vs. context session) and target position (between- vs. within-cycle, defined by the context) (F(1, 15)=7. 151, p=0.017, ηp2 = 0.323).

claim: Feature-based temporal structure of an auditory stream, although being task-irrelevant, could systematically modulate the allocation of visual attention over the AB stream.
source: Results from Experiment 1a demonstrated that feature-based temporal structure of an auditory stream, although being task-irrelevant, could systematically modulate the allocation of visual attention over the AB stream.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results from Experiment 1a.

claim: When two targets were located in distinct cycles, they were accompanied by different tones, in contrast to that when located within the same cycle they were accompanied by the same tone.
source: Since the temporal structure of the contextual sounds was defined by periodic changes of pitch, when two targets were located in distinct cycles as in the between-cycle condition, they were accompanied by different tones, in contrast to that when located within the same cycle they were accompanied by the same tone.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and stimulus characteristics.

claim: In Experiment 1b, despite that the sounds paired with the targets were exactly the same as in Experiment 1a, the difference in T2 detection accuracy caused by the contextual sounds was no longer observed (t(15) = 0.433, p=0.671, Cohen's d = 0.108).
source: Despite that the sounds paired with the targets were exactly the same as in Experiment 1a, the difference in T2 detection accuracy caused by the contextual sounds was no longer observed (t(15) = 0.433, p=0.671, Cohen's d = 0.108), neither was its interaction with experimental session (F(1, 15)=2.734, p=0.119, ηp2 = 0.154; Figure 1C).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 1C.

claim: In Experiment 1b, the interaction between experimental session and target position was not significant (F(1, 15)=2.734, p=0.119, ηp2 = 0.154).

claim: It is the temporal structure of the contextual sounds, not the pitch difference at target presentation, that accounts for the between-cycle facilitation effect observed in Experiment 1a.
source: In other words, T2 was identified with similar accuracy across all the conditions in Experiment 1b, suggesting that it is the temporal structure of the contextual sounds, not the pitch difference at target presentation, that accounts for the between-cycle facilitation effect observed in Experiment 1a.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results of Experiments 1a and 1b.

claim: In Experiment 1a, the auditory context always changed its pitch value every four items, that is every 400 ms as one cycle, resulting in rhythmic cycles at 2.5 Hz.
source: In Experiment 1a, the auditory context always changed its pitch value every four items, that is every 400 ms as one cycle, resulting in rhythmic cycles at 2.5 Hz.

claim: For both 2 Hz and 3.3 Hz context frequencies, the T2 detection performance in the between-cycle condition was significantly higher than that in the within-cycle condition (for 2 Hz, t(15) = 3.478, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.869; for 3.3 Hz, t(15) = 2.467, p=0.030, Cohen's d = 0.617).
source: For both context frequencies, the T2 detection performance in the between-cycle condition was significantly higher than that in the within-cycle condition (Figure 2B; for 2 Hz, t(15) = 3.478, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.869; for 3.3 Hz, t(15) = 2.467, p=0.030, Cohen's d = 0.617), suggesting successful attentional modulation effects.

claim: In Experiment 1e, when the stimulus onset timing was randomized, T2 detection performance in the between-cycle condition was no longer improved relative to the within-cycle condition (t(15) = 0.302, p=0.767, Cohen's d = 0.076).
source: In line with our speculation, when the stimulus onset timing was randomized, T2 detection performance in the between-cycle condition was no longer improved relative to the within-cycle condition (Figure 2D, Irreg-T; t(15) = 0.302, p=0.767, Cohen's d = 0.076), despite the potential benefit of the grouping effect.
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 2D.

claim: The absence of context-induced modulation effect in Experiments 1d and 1e consistently supports the idea that temporal grouping without dynamic attending guided by feature- and timing-related regularities in the auditory context is insufficient to cause the behavioral modulation effect.
source: Putting together, the absence of context-induced modulation effect in Experiments 1d and 1e consistently supports the idea that temporal grouping without dynamic attending guided by feature- and timing-related regularities in the auditory context is insufficient to cause the behavioral modulation effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of Experiments 1d and 1e.

claim: Information from the auditory modality, like speech and music, is inherently organized in time and provides rich sources of rhythmic structures that can be proactively tracked by the human brain.
source: Information from the auditory modality, like speech and music, is inherently organized in time and provides rich sources of rhythmic structures that can be proactively tracked by the human brain (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Haegens and Zion Golumbic, 2018; Zion Golumbic et al., 2012).

source: First of all, we replicated the behavioral modulation effect that T2 performance was significantly better in the between-cycle condition versus the within-cycle condition, only in the context session (between-cycle: 0.567 ± 0.036, within-cycle: 0.520 ± 0.039, t(15) = 3.838, p=0.002, Cohen's d = 0.960) but not in the baseline session (between-cycle: 0.519 ± 0.039, within-cycle: 0.527 ± 0.043, t(15) = 0.296, p=0.771, Cohen's d = 0.074).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the EEG experiment.

claim: In the EEG experiment, the behavioral modulation effect was not observed in the baseline session (between-cycle: 0.519 ± 0.039, within-cycle: 0.527 ± 0.043, t(15) = 0.296, p=0.771, Cohen's d = 0.074).
source: First of all, we replicated the behavioral modulation effect that T2 performance was significantly better in the between-cycle condition versus the within-cycle condition, only in the context session (between-cycle: 0.567 ± 0.036, within-cycle: 0.520 ± 0.039, t(15) = 3.838, p=0.002, Cohen's d = 0.960) but not in the baseline session (between-cycle: 0.519 ± 0.039, within-cycle: 0.527 ± 0.043, t(15) = 0.296, p=0.771, Cohen's d = 0.074).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the EEG experiment.

claim: The highest power spectrum peak in the context session was at 10 Hz (t(15) = 10.610, p<0.001, FDR-corrected).
source: Power spectrum in Figure 4A shows several peaks for the context session, with the highest at 10 Hz (compared with zero using one-sample t-test, right-tailed, t(15) = 10.610, p<0.001, FDR-corrected for multiple comparisons across frequencies) corresponding to the common stimulation frequency of the visual and auditory streams.
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 4A.

claim: The 10 Hz power peak corresponds to the common stimulation frequency of the visual and auditory streams.
source: Power spectrum in Figure 4A shows several peaks for the context session, with the highest at 10 Hz (compared with zero using one-sample t-test, right-tailed, t(15) = 10.610, p<0.001, FDR-corrected for multiple comparisons across frequencies) corresponding to the common stimulation frequency of the visual and auditory streams.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 10 Hz peak based on the experimental design.

claim: The second-highest power peak appeared at 2.5 Hz (t(15) = 5.730, p<0.001, FDR-corrected), followed by its harmonics at 5 and 7.5 Hz.
source: More importantly, the second-highest peak appeared at 2.5 Hz (t(15) = 5.730, p<0.001, FDR-corrected), followed by its harmonics at 5 and 7.5 Hz, indicating neural tracking of the feature-defined structure of the auditory context.
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the EEG experiment.

claim: The 2.5 Hz power peak and its harmonics indicate neural tracking of the feature-defined structure of the auditory context.
source: More importantly, the second-highest peak appeared at 2.5 Hz (t(15) = 5.730, p<0.001, FDR-corrected), followed by its harmonics at 5 and 7.5 Hz, indicating neural tracking of the feature-defined structure of the auditory context.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 2.5 Hz peak based on the experimental design.

claim: In the baseline session, a significant power peak was found at 10 Hz (t(15) = 9.405, p<0.001, FDR-corrected), but not at 2.5 Hz (t(15) = 0.301, p=0.384, FDR-corrected).
source: In contrast with the observation in the context session, we only found significant power peak at 10 Hz (t(15) = 9.405, p<0.001, FDR-corrected), but not at 2.5 Hz (t(15) = 0.301, p=0.384, FDR-corrected) in the baseline session where contextual rhythms were absent, and the power at 2.5 Hz was significantly weaker than that in the context session (t(15) = 3.421, p=0.002, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the EEG experiment.

claim: The power at 2.5 Hz was significantly weaker in the baseline session than in the context session (t(15) = 3.421, p=0.002, FDR-corrected).
source: In contrast with the observation in the context session, we only found significant power peak at 10 Hz (t(15) = 9.405, p<0.001, FDR-corrected), but not at 2.5 Hz (t(15) = 0.301, p=0.384, FDR-corrected) in the baseline session where contextual rhythms were absent, and the power at 2.5 Hz was significantly weaker than that in the context session (t(15) = 3.421, p=0.002, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the EEG experiment.

claim: The brain can entrain to the higher-order structure defined by changes in an auditory feature (i.e. pitch) of the contextual stream.
source: The significant enhancement of EEG power at 2.5 Hz clearly demonstrates that the brain can entrain to the higher-order structure defined by changes in an auditory feature (i.e. pitch) of the contextual stream.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 2.5 Hz power enhancement observed in the EEG data.

claim: There is a wide range of individual variation in cortical tracking of contextual rhythms.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we also observed a wide range of individual variation in such cortical tracking of contextual rhythms (Grahn and McAuley, 2009; Kranczioch, 2017; Nozaradan et al., 2016).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to previous studies and the current data.

claim: In the context session, two significant clusters showed positive correlation between power at 2.5 Hz and individuals' behavioral effect—one in the parieto-occipital region (P5, PO7, PO5, PO3; r = 0.587, p=0.008, right-tailed) and the other in the frontal area (F3, F1, FZ, FC3, FC1, FCZ, C1, CZ; r = 0.681, p=0.002).
source: In the context session, we identified two significant clusters showing positive correlation between power at 2.5 Hz and individuals' behavioral effect—one in the parieto-occipital region (Figure 4B; P5, PO7, PO5, PO3; r = 0.587, p=0.008, right-tailed) and the other in the frontal area (F3, F1, FZ, FC3, FC1, FCZ, C1, CZ; r = 0.681, p=0.002).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 4B.

claim: No significant clusters showing correlation between 2.5 Hz power and behavioral effect were found in the baseline session (p>0.05).
source: By contrast, no significant clusters were found in the baseline session (p>0.05).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the EEG experiment.

claim: ITPC in the context session peaked at 2.5 and 10 Hz, suggesting a hierarchical entrainment effect elicited by both feature-based and time-based regularities.
source: Consistent with the power spectrum, ITPC in the context session peaked at 2.5 and 10 Hz (Figure 4C), suggesting a hierarchical entrainment effect elicited by both feature-based and time-based regularities.
evidence: This reports ITPC results and references Figure 4C.

claim: ITPC in the baseline session only peaked at 10 Hz, mirroring the stimulation rate of the visual stream.
source: By contrast, ITPC in the baseline session only peaked at 10 Hz, mirroring the stimulation rate of the visual stream, and the ITPC at 2.5 Hz was significantly weaker than that in the context session (t(15) = 4.652, p<0.001, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This reports ITPC results from the baseline session.

claim: The ITPC at 2.5 Hz was significantly weaker in the baseline session than in the context session (t(15) = 4.652, p<0.001, FDR-corrected).
source: By contrast, ITPC in the baseline session only peaked at 10 Hz, mirroring the stimulation rate of the visual stream, and the ITPC at 2.5 Hz was significantly weaker than that in the context session (t(15) = 4.652, p<0.001, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the EEG experiment.

claim: Only in the context session, the 2.5 Hz ITPC was positively correlated with the behavioral modulation index, yielding two significant clusters in the parieto-occipital area (P7, P5, PO7, PO5, PO3, O1: r = 0.612, p=0.006) and the frontal area (FPZ, FP2, AF4, F2, F4, F6; r = 0.672, p=0.002).
source: Critically, only in the context session, the 2.5 Hz ITPC was positively correlated with the behavioral modulation index, yielding two significant clusters in the parieto-occipital area (Figure 4D; P7, P5, PO7, PO5, PO3, O1: r = 0.612, p=0.006) and the frontal area (FPZ, FP2, AF4, F2, F4, F6; r = 0.672, p=0.002).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 4D.

claim: The better one's brain oscillations entrain to the higher-order temporal structure of the contextual rhythms, the larger attentional enhancement one may exhibit in the between-cycle condition over the within-cycle condition.
source: Taken together, the results of 2.5 Hz power and ITPC jointly demonstrate that the better one's brain oscillations entrain to the higher-order temporal structure of the contextual rhythms, the larger attentional enhancement one may exhibit in the between-cycle condition over the within-cycle condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analyses of 2.5 Hz power and ITPC with behavioral effects.

claim: Alpha oscillations have been considered to play a crucial and even causal role in temporal attention, particularly in the AB effect.
source: Alpha oscillations have been considered to play a crucial and even causal role in temporal attention, particularly in the AB effect (Hanslmayr et al., 2011; Klimesch, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: An increase in alpha power at the stimulus frequency indicated attentional orienting to the stimulus stream, providing an online measure of attentional allocation over the RSVP stream.
source: It has been demonstrated that an increase in alpha power at the stimulus frequency indicated attentional orienting to the stimulus stream, providing an online measure of attentional allocation over the RSVP stream (Müller and Hübner, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Enhanced alpha power at stimulus rate in the AB task has been shown to be associated with correct T2 detection.
source: On the other hand, enhanced alpha power at stimulus rate in the AB task has also been shown to be associated with correct T2 detection (Janson et al., 2014; Keil et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Two significant clusters showed stronger 10 Hz alpha power in the between-cycle condition than in the within-cycle condition for the context session—one in the left parieto-occipital region (T7, C5, C3, TP7, CP5, CP3, P5, P3, PO5, PO3, O1; t(15) = 3.570, p=0.0014) and the other in a right-lateralized region (AF4, F2, F4, FC4, FC6, FT8, C4, C6, T8, CP4, CP6, TP8, P8; t(15) = 3.631, p=0.0012).
source: We calculated alpha power around the stimulation frequency (9.5–10.5 Hz) within the time window of 0–100 ms after T2 onset, and found two significant clusters for the context session—one in the left parieto-occipital region (Figure 5A; T7, C5, C3, TP7, CP5, CP3, P5, P3, PO5, PO3, O1) and the other in a right-lateralized region (AF4, F2, F4, FC4, FC6, FT8, C4, C6, T8, CP4, CP6, TP8, P8), both showing stronger 10 Hz alpha power in the between-cycle condition than in the within-cycle condition (for the left cluster, t(15) = 3.570, p=0.0014; for the right cluster, t(15) = 3.631, p=0.0012, right-tailed, cluster-based permutation test).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 5A.

claim: The 10 Hz alpha power within the time window of −100–0 ms prior to T2 onset showed an enhancement for the between-cycle condition relative to the within-cycle condition in the left parieto-occipital cluster (CP3, CP5, P3, P5, PO3, PO5, POZ, O1, OZ; t(15) = 2.774, p=0.007).
source: Results revealed an enhancement of this pre-T2 neural response for the between-cycle condition relative to the within-cycle condition, which is similar to that observed within the post-T2 time window but more restricted to the left parieto-occipital cluster (Figure 5A; CP3, CP5, P3, P5, PO3, PO5, POZ, O1, OZ; t(15) = 2.774, p=0.007).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 5A.

claim: Cross-frequency coupling between delta phase and alpha power has been found to support the attentional selection between competing stimuli.
source: To address this question, we analyzed cross-frequency coupling between delta phase and alpha power, which has been found to support the attentional selection between competing stimuli (Gomez-Ramirez et al., 2011; Wilson and Foxe, 2020; Wöstmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The modulation index (MI) of phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) between delta (1.5–3.5 Hz) and alpha band (7–13 Hz) was stronger in the between-cycle condition than in the within-cycle condition in the parieto-occipital region (t(15) = 2.432, p=0.028).
source: The MI was stronger in the between-cycle condition than in the within-cycle condition, while the effect reached significance only in the parieto-occipital region (Figure 5B; t(15) = 2.432, p=0.028) but not in the frontal region (t(15) = 1.459, p=0.165).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 5B.

claim: The modulation index (MI) of phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) between delta (1.5–3.5 Hz) and alpha band (7–13 Hz) was not significantly different between conditions in the frontal region (t(15) = 1.459, p=0.165).
source: The MI was stronger in the between-cycle condition than in the within-cycle condition, while the effect reached significance only in the parieto-occipital region (Figure 5B; t(15) = 2.432, p=0.028) but not in the frontal region (t(15) = 1.459, p=0.165).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 5B.

claim: The contrast effect of delta-alpha PAC showed a positive correlation with the attentional modulation effect on behavioral performance in the parieto-occipital region (r = 0.660, p=0.005).
source: More importantly, this contrast effect of delta-alpha PAC showed a positive correlation with the attentional modulation effect on behavioral performance, which was also restricted to the parieto-occipital region (Figure 5C; r = 0.660, p=0.005) and not found in the frontal region (r = 0.154, p=0.569).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 5C.

claim: The contrast effect of delta-alpha PAC did not show a significant correlation with the attentional modulation effect in the frontal region (r = 0.154, p=0.569).
source: More importantly, this contrast effect of delta-alpha PAC showed a positive correlation with the attentional modulation effect on behavioral performance, which was also restricted to the parieto-occipital region (Figure 5C; r = 0.660, p=0.005) and not found in the frontal region (r = 0.154, p=0.569).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results and references Figure 5C.

claim: A cluster-based permutation test yielded a positively significant cluster in the parieto-occipital region (PO7, PO5, PO3, O1, OZ; r = 0.697, p=0.003) for the correlation between delta-alpha PAC and behavioral modulation.
source: To further confirm the association between the delta-alpha PAC and the observed attentional modulation effect, we did a cluster-based permutation test, which again yielded a positively significant cluster in the parieto-occipital region (PO7, PO5, PO3, O1, OZ; r = 0.697, p=0.003).
evidence: This reports specific statistical results from the EEG experiment.

claim: Cortical tracking of hierarchical temporal structures of the auditory context, as well as the coordination of such cortical tracking effects in delta and alpha bands, may play a vital role in reconstructing the deployment of visual attention in the AB task.
source: These results, combined with the findings from single-band analyses, indicate that cortical tracking of hierarchical temporal structures of the auditory context, as well as the coordination of such cortical tracking effects in delta and alpha bands, may play a vital role in reconstructing the deployment of visual attention in the AB task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined EEG results.

claim: Dynamic information flows, such as speech and music, are composed of rhythmic structures nested across multiple timescales.
source: Dynamic information flows, such as speech and music, are composed of rhythmic structures nested across multiple timescales (Ding et al., 2016; Gross et al., 2013; Koelsch et al., 2013; Peelle and Davis, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hierarchical structures in dynamic information are organized in time based on regularities in stimulus timing (time-based) and regularities in information content (feature-based).
source: These hierarchical structures are organized in time based on regularities in stimulus timing, that is, when sensory signals are emitted (time-based), as well as regularities in information content, that is, how physical or semantic features of the sensory inputs change over time (feature-based).
evidence: This describes the conceptual framework for understanding hierarchical temporal structures.

claim: Temporal structures formed by time-based regularities are effective in directing attention and enhance information selection at the expected time points.
source: Accrued evidence suggests that temporal structures formed by time-based regularities are effective in directing attention and enhance information selection at the expected time points (Jones et al., 2002; Nobre et al., 2007; Nobre and van Ede, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The attentional modulation effect did not occur in the absence of regular stimulus timing.
source: It is worth noting that the attentional modulation effect did not occur in the absence of regular stimulus timing.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 1e where irregular timing abolished the effect.

claim: The feature-based regularities should work in tandem with the time-based regularities to reconstruct the dynamics of visual temporal attention, at least under the current experimental settings.
source: In other words, the feature-based regularities should work in tandem with the time-based regularities to reconstruct the dynamics of visual temporal attention, at least under the current experimental settings.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing both types of regularities are necessary.

claim: Temporal regularities embedded in information content can act along with the time-based anticipation in attentional guidance.
source: It has been suggested by studies using auditory materials, mostly in speech and music perception, that temporal regularities embedded in information content can act along with the time-based anticipation in attentional guidance (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Morillon et al., 2016; Peelle and Davis, 2012; Zion Golumbic et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The findings extend previous studies by establishing a mechanism in visual temporal attention that is guided by regularities in feature-defined structures on top of the anticipation based on stimulation timing.
source: Our findings extend these studies by establishing a mechanism in visual temporal attention that is guided by regularities in feature-defined structures on top of the anticipation based on stimulation timing.
evidence: This is an inference about the contribution of the current study to the field.

claim: The AB phenomenon represents a bottleneck of conscious awareness pertaining to the temporal resolution of visual attention.
source: The AB phenomenon represents a bottleneck of conscious awareness pertaining to the temporal resolution of visual attention.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of the AB phenomenon in the literature.

claim: Even long repetitive training cannot eliminate the AB effect.
source: It is well known for its robustness that even long repetitive training cannot eliminate the AB effect (Braun, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Some studies have demonstrated attenuated AB magnitude by enhancing T2 salience with color-salience training, emotional arousal, or concurrent sounds.
source: Some studies have demonstrated attenuated AB magnitude, as manifested in increased T2 detectability, by enhancing T2 salience with color-salience training (Choi et al., 2012), emotional arousal (Keil and Ihssen, 2004), or concurrent sounds (Olivers and Van der Burg, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Improved T2 performance has been reported when explicitly cueing the target-onset-asynchrony (TOA) on a trial-by-trial basis or manipulating the predictability of target onset.
source: Another line of research has also reported improved T2 performance when explicitly cueing the target-onset-asynchrony (TOA) on a trial-by-trial basis (Martens and Johnson, 2005) or manipulating the predictability of target onset (Tang et al., 2014; Visser et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the current study, the salience of targets and temporal expectations about T2 onset were comparable across all experimental conditions.
source: By contrast, in our study, the salience of targets and temporal expectations about T2 onset were comparable across all experimental conditions.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: When T1 and T2 were separated in different cycles, the temporal relations between them were reframed, which might at least partially reduce the competition between the targets.
source: In particular, when T1 and T2 were separated in different cycles, the temporal relations between them were reframed, which might at least partially reduce the competition between the targets, thus improving the resolution of visual temporal attention and boosting the conscious access to T2.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: Neural oscillations can be entrained to external rhythms across different frequencies.
source: Neural oscillations can be entrained to external rhythms across different frequencies (Calderone et al., 2014; Escoffier et al., 2015; Henry et al., 2014; Mathewson et al., 2012; Schroeder et al., 2010; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Thut et al., 2011), allowing the brain to encode dynamic information with multiplexed rhythmic structures across different timescales (Fontolan et al., 2014; Lakatos et al., 2005; O'Connell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The linguistic structure possesses a temporal hierarchy—from smaller phonetic elements to larger syllabic and phrasal units, which correspondingly elicit neural entrainment at multiple frequency bands.
source: The linguistic structure possesses a temporal hierarchy—from smaller phonetic elements to larger syllabic and phrasal units, which correspondingly elicit neural entrainment at multiple frequency bands (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Zion Golumbic et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on speech processing.

claim: There is growing evidence that cortical tracking of the higher-order temporal structures plays a vital role in speech comprehension.
source: Moreover, there is growing evidence that cortical tracking of the higher-order temporal structures plays a vital role in speech comprehension (Ding et al., 2016; Gross et al., 2013; Peelle and Davis, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The hierarchical entrainment observed in the current study does not rely on previously acquired knowledge about the structured information and can be established automatically even when the higher-order structure comes from a task-irrelevant and cross-modal contextual rhythm.
source: This effect, distinct from the hierarchical entrainment to speech signals, does not rely on previously acquired knowledge about the structured information and can be established automatically even when the higher-order structure comes from a task-irrelevant and cross-modal contextual rhythm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental design and results.

claim: The scalp topographic map of correlation between 2.5 Hz entrainment and behavioral modulation is lateralized and restricted to the left parietal region, which was found to be associated with temporal attention.
source: The scalp topographic map of correlation is lateralized and restricted to the left parietal region, which was found to be associated with temporal attention (Bolger et al., 2014; Coull and Nobre, 1998).
evidence: This describes the spatial pattern of the correlation and is supported by citations to previous research on temporal attention.

claim: The cortical tracking of feature-based contextual structure is critical to the redeployment of attentional resources over the AB stream and may lead to the behavioral modulation effect.
source: These findings are in good accordance with our assumption that the cortical tracking of feature-based contextual structure is critical to the redeployment of attentional resources over the AB stream and may lead to the behavioral modulation effect, which sheds fresh light on the adaptive value of the structure-based entrainment effect by expanding its role from rhythmic information (e.g. speech) perception to temporal attention deployment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between neural entrainment and behavioral effects.

claim: There has been a debate about whether the neural alignment to rhythmic stimulation reflects active entrainment of endogenous oscillatory processes (i.e. induced activity) or a series of passively evoked steady-state responses.
source: There has been a debate about whether the neural alignment to rhythmic stimulation reflects active entrainment of endogenous oscillatory processes (i.e. induced activity) or a series of passively evoked steady-state responses (Keitel et al., 2019; Notbohm et al., 2016; Zoefel et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes an ongoing debate in the field and is supported by citations.

claim: The study demonstrated an attention-related neural tracking of the higher-order temporal structure based on the induced power at 2.5 Hz.
source: In addition to the observation of evoked responses to the contextual structure, we also demonstrated an attention-related neural tracking of the higher-order temporal structure based on the induced power at 2.5 Hz (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the observed attentional modulation effect is at least partially derived from the entrainment of intrinsic oscillatory brain activity.
evidence: This reports additional analysis results and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed attentional modulation effect is at least partially derived from the entrainment of intrinsic oscillatory brain activity.
source: In addition to the observation of evoked responses to the contextual structure, we also demonstrated an attention-related neural tracking of the higher-order temporal structure based on the induced power at 2.5 Hz (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the observed attentional modulation effect is at least partially derived from the entrainment of intrinsic oscillatory brain activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the induced power analysis.

claim: A widely accepted function of alpha activity in attention is that alpha oscillations suppress irrelevant visual information during spatial selection.
source: A widely accepted function of alpha activity in attention is that alpha oscillations suppress irrelevant visual information during spatial selection (Kelly et al., 2006; Thut et al., 2006; Worden et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The currently observed increase in alpha power for the between-cycle condition may reflect more of the stimulus-driven processes related to attentional enhancement.
source: According to these findings, the currently observed increase in alpha power for the between-cycle condition may reflect more of the stimulus-driven processes related to attentional enhancement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the alpha power results based on previous findings.

claim: In the left parieto-occipital cluster that exhibits phase-locked neural responses to both feature-based contextual structures at 2.5 Hz and first-order stimulus frequency at 10 Hz, there is an enhancement of phase-amplitude coupling between the delta and alpha oscillations for the between- relative to the within-cycle condition.
source: Further analysis reveals that, in the left parieto-occipital cluster that exhibits phase-locked neural responses to both feature-based contextual structures at 2.5 Hz and first-order stimulus frequency at 10 Hz, there is an enhancement of phase-amplitude coupling between the delta and alpha oscillations for the between- relative to the within-cycle condition.
evidence: This reports the results of the phase-amplitude coupling analysis.

claim: The strength of delta-alpha coupling enhancement predicts the effect of higher-order temporal structures on dynamic attentional allocation at the individual level.
source: Moreover, the strength of this delta-alpha coupling enhancement predicts the effect of higher-order temporal structures on dynamic attentional allocation at the individual level.
evidence: This reports the correlation between PAC and behavioral effects.

claim: Neural entrainment to a slower external rhythm may serve as a mechanism of attentional deployment, with the phase of delta oscillation regulating the excitability of neural activity in the alpha band.
source: These findings corroborate the idea that neural entrainment to a slower external rhythm may serve as a mechanism of attentional deployment, with the phase of delta oscillation regulating the excitability of neural activity in the alpha band (Gomez-Ramirez et al., 2011; Wilson and Foxe, 2020; Wöstmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PAC results supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The DAT assumes attention to be inherently oscillatory and can be driven by the timing pattern of external events.
source: The DAT assumes attention to be inherently oscillatory and can be driven by the timing pattern of external events (Jones, 1976; Jones et al., 1982; Jones and Boltz, 1989; Large and Jones, 1999).
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework of DAT and is supported by citations.

claim: The internal attentional oscillation may not only align with first-order rhythmic structures based on stimulus timing, but also with higher-order rhythmic structures defined by content-based changes of the information flow.
source: Primarily, our behavioral observations suggest that to utilize regularities in a hierarchical temporal structure, the internal attentional oscillation may not only align with first-order rhythmic structures based on stimulus timing, but also with higher-order rhythmic structures defined by content-based changes of the information flow.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results of the study.

claim: The dynamic attending process necessitates the synergy between time- and content-based regularities, which could be implemented by neural entrainment to the higher-order temporal structure and its coordination with the cortical tracking of the stimulus rhythm through cross-frequency coupling.
source: Such a dynamic attending process necessitates the synergy between time- and content-based regularities, which could be implemented by neural entrainment to the higher-order temporal structure and its coordination with the cortical tracking of the stimulus rhythm through cross-frequency coupling.
evidence: This is an inference about the neural mechanisms based on the combined behavioral and EEG results.

claim: Feature-defined contextual rhythms play a role in reconstructing the deployment of visual attention along dynamic information streams.
source: In summary, the current study emphasizes the role of feature-defined contextual rhythms in reconstructing the deployment of visual attention along dynamic information streams.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding of the study.

claim: When examining the perception of complex dynamic information, temporal context on multiple timescales should be taken into consideration because it provides a meaningful hierarchical temporal frame for attentional deployment.
source: Taking the AB phenomenon as an example, we provide a new perspective on visual temporal attention research—when examining the perception of complex dynamic information, temporal context on multiple timescales should be taken into consideration because it provides a meaningful hierarchical temporal frame for attentional deployment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The temporal frame, implemented by neural entrainment, may serve to organize attentional resources in a prospective manner and help construct our conscious experience of the world in the dimension of time.
source: This temporal frame, implemented by neural entrainment, may serve to organize attentional resources in a prospective manner and help construct our conscious experience of the world in the dimension of time.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: A total of 144 volunteers (aged from 18 to 30 years, 69 females) were recruited and paid for their participation in the current study.
source: A total of 144 volunteers (aged from 18 to 30 years, 69 females) were recruited and paid for their participation in the current study.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: One hundred and twenty-eight participants participated in the behavioral Experiments 1a-1e, 2a-2b, and 3 (16 for each experiment, with participants' gender balanced).
source: One hundred and twenty-eight participated in the behavioral Experiments 1a-1e, 2a-2b, and 3 (16 for each experiment, with participants' gender balanced), and 16 (5 females) in the EEG experiment.
evidence: This describes the participant distribution across experiments.

claim: 16 participants (5 females) participated in the EEG experiment.
source: One hundred and twenty-eight participated in the behavioral Experiments 1a-1e, 2a-2b, and 3 (16 for each experiment, with participants' gender balanced), and 16 (5 females) in the EEG experiment.
evidence: This describes the participant sample for the EEG experiment.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and normal hearing and were naïve to the purpose of the experiment.
source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and normal hearing and were naïve to the purpose of the experiment.

claim: Only participants who exhibited a typical AB effect during a pre-screening session were asked to take part in the formal experiments.
source: Considering the individual differences in the AB effect, only participants who exhibited a typical AB effect (i.e. an impairment of T2 accuracy at short lags compared with that at long lags) during a pre-screening session were asked to take part in the formal experiments.
evidence: This describes the participant selection procedure.
